segments.text: Our laboratory circuit has a battery, switch, copper wire, resistor, and a series ammeter.
Now let us look inside the copper wire and see what happens at the atomic level.
Copper ions vibrate in place, while electrons move randomly.
Close the switch. Electrons drift right, creating a magnetic field.
Electrons drift from negative to positive. The green circles remain because current is still flowing.
Circles represent the field around our circuit.
Conventional current flows the opposite way.
The compass needle turns, detecting the wire's magnetic field.
Half an ampere: twenty-five degrees of deflection.
Same distance: double current doubles field strength.
One ampere: stronger field, forty-three degrees of deflection.
To summarize what we have learned: current creates a magnetic field. More current makes it stronger. Without net electron flow, the wire's field disappears.
